newsitem.title: BELARUS: Lukashenko tightens his grip on Belarus.
newsitem.headline: Lukashenko tightens his grip on Belarus.

text.p: President Alexander Lukashenko, tightening his grip on Belarus, prepared on Wednesday to push his opponents out of the parliament building -- using painters and electricians rather than riot police.

Belarus has two rival parliaments since Lukashenko's victory in Sunday's referendum, pronounced illegal by Europe's top human rights body, but the balance swung further in the president's favour on Wednesday.
Facing defiance from a rump of several dozen deputies occupying the old parliament, Lukashenko's supporters indicated he would try to get them out by renovating their workplace.
"We must ask his administration to renovate the Oval Hall urgently," deputy Yuri Pashkevich told 114 pro-Lukashenko deputies meeting in a separate building.

Deputies backing the president abolished the old parliament amid rousing applause under Lukashenko's approving gaze and approved the formation of a new, 110-seat lower house. An upper house is also planned.

"This is a historic moment," Lukashenko said as he signed the bills into law. "I am bound to you as you are to me. I want people to say at the end of your term: 'We do not need elections. Let's keep these deputies'."
Lukashenko will sign the new constitution at a ceremony on Thursday afternoon.

Members of the rump parliament said phone lines linking their chamber to the president and the government had been cut but a Council of Europe delegation recognised the rump as the legal legislature, declared the referendum illegal and said the new constitution "fell short of minimum democratic standards".
Delegation leader Tadeusz Iwinski of Poland told reporters at the old parliament that Belarus should be ready for anything.
"The worst case scenario would be the use of force...but the best scenario would be to introduce the rule of law," he said.
Opposition deputies had been expressing fear that Lukashenko might get them out by force, as in April 1995, when hunger-striking deputies were beaten out of the chamber.
But liberal deputy Anatoly Lebedko said that "a violent solution would not suit the president."

Iwinski, whose delegation was invited by the old parliament's speaker Semyon Sharetsky, said they had met Lukashenko for two hours but the conversation "instead of dialogue, consisted of two monologues".

Russia, Belarus's most powerful ally and its biggest creditor, sent a clear message of support to Minsk on Wednesday when it despatched Defence Minister Igor Rodionov to a ceremony to mark the withdrawal to Russia of the last Soviet-era nuclear missile on Belarussian territory.
The ceremony marked the final withdrawal of nuclear weapons from former Soviet territory to Russia. The actual warheads had already left.
Interfax news agency reported from Minsk that Lukashenko had received a "congratulatory telegram" from Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, in which he backed the new constitution.
The agency gave no source for the report. It was not immediately possible to confirm it. Chernomyrdin was in Paris for an official visit.
